“If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them ... I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump said when delivering the keynote speech at a Republican convention in Dallas.
He added that the only caveat with the dividend would be that it must be spent in the United States. Trump did not provide any more details on the potential payout.

title: Gold holds near $4,400 as traders await inflation data for Fed clues
full_text:
U.S. stocks end lower, bonds slide as Treasury buyback disappoints, oil tops $100
Investing.com -- Gold prices were little changed on Thursday as investors awaited U.S. inflation data for clues on whether the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its meeting next week.
Higher Treasury yields and renewed Middle East tensions remain near term headwinds, although a softer dollar and longer term demand for bullion continue to offer support.
At 20:43 ET (00:43 GMT), XAU/USD fell 0.1% to $4,398.53 an ounce, while Gold Futures declined 0.4% to $4,442.00. XAG/USD was little changed at $67.28 an ounce, while XPT/USD fell 0.6% to $1,888.23. The U.S. Dollar Index was little changed at 98.81.
Treasury yields, Middle East tensions keep pressure on gold
Gold has traded in a relatively narrow range around $4,400 in recent weeks after rebounding from a floor near $4,000 in July.
Investors have continued to weigh the metal's longer term appeal as a portfolio hedge against near term pressure from higher bond yields and worsening tensions in the Middle East.
U.S. 10-year Treasury yields rose after the government's latest plan to buy as much as $6 billion of longer dated debt failed to sway the bond market. Higher yields can weigh on gold because bullion pays no interest.
Oil prices also remain a concern. Brent crude reached $100 a barrel for the first time since July.
The war is now in its seventh month, and Iran has warned it is prepared for a more intense conflict if the United States continues attacks on its territory and infrastructure.
PPI, CPI set to test Fed rate outlook
Markets are now focused on Thursday's U.S. producer price index and Friday's consumer price index ahead of the Fed's policy meeting. Swaps markets are pricing about a 65% probability of a rate hike this month.
Tony Sycamore, senior market analyst at IG, said gold finished higher overnight at around $4,402, helped by a weaker dollar even as U.S. bond yields rose sharply.
Sycamore said gold remains well below its 200-day moving average at around $4,537. The metal needs to reclaim that level to signal that the pullback from the $4,697 high has ended and that the broader uptrend has resumed.
Investor demand has also strengthened, with global gold-backed ETFs attracting $18 billion in August, their second-largest monthly inflow on record, the World Gold Council said. Holdings rose by 121 tonnes to a record 4,189 tonnes, while assets under management climbed 16% to $615 billion.
North American funds recorded their third-largest monthly inflow on record, while European-listed funds posted their largest ever monthly inflow, the World Gold Council said.

title: Justice Department probes Nvidia’s Groq deal over antitrust concerns - NYT
full_text:
U.S. stocks end lower, bonds slide as Treasury buyback disappoints, oil tops $100
Investing.com -- The U.S. Justice Department is investigating whether Nvidia’s deal with artificial intelligence chipmaker Groq was structured to avoid antitrust scrutiny, The New York Times reported on Wednesday, citing two people familiar with the inquiry.
The investigation began shortly after Nvidia announced the agreement in December, and the Justice Department has since sent Nvidia a formal demand for information, according to the report.
The agency could fine Nvidia if it finds wrongdoing, although officials do not currently expect the deal to be unwound. The inquiry remains ongoing and could end without any enforcement action.
The scrutiny centers on an arrangement Groq described as a nonexclusive licensing agreement that gave Nvidia access to its custom chips designed for AI inference. As part of the deal, Groq Chief Executive Jonathan Ross and Chief Operating Officer Sunny Madra joined Nvidia.
The case highlights growing regulatory attention on AI industry deals that combine technology licensing with the hiring of key employees without an outright acquisition.
Such structures can avoid the automatic government reviews that typically apply to traditional mergers and acquisitions, even as they may give larger technology companies access to critical talent and intellectual property.
Groq remains an independent business and continues to sell cloud-computing services. The company announced in August that it was raising $350 million in new funding, with Nvidia planning to participate, underscoring the unusual structure of its relationship with the chipmaker.
Nvidia has defended the arrangement, according to the report.
The probe comes as Nvidia’s dominance in AI chips gives it enormous influence across the industry. The New York Times said the company, with a market value of about $5.4 trillion, has increasingly used its financial strength to invest in AI startups and support customers.
Groq was last valued at $7 billion before its arrangement with Nvidia, according to PitchBook. Its investors include Samsung, BlackRock and 1789 Capital.

U.S. stocks end lower, bonds slide as Treasury buyback disappoints, oil tops $100
Investing.com-- U.S. stock futures were steady Wednesday evening after Wall Street ended lower, as rising Treasury yields and oil prices above $100 a barrel kept investors cautious ahead of key U.S. inflation data that could shape expectations for the Federal Reserve’s policy decision next week.
S&P 500 Futures inched 0.1% higher to 7,654.50 points, while Nasdaq 100 Futures also gained 0.1% to 29,472.75 points by 20:33 ET (00:33 GMT). Dow Jones Futures were up 0.2% at 52,535.0 points.
The muted futures trading followed a broad decline in U.S. equities. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.8%, the S&P 500 lost 0.5%, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.6%, marking a third straight session of losses for the major indexes.

Higher oil prices have revived concerns that an extended energy shock could keep inflation elevated and make it harder for the Fed to ease monetary policy.

title: Pilot pressed on with landing despite warnings in Miami cargo crash, NTSB says
full_text:
U.S. stocks end lower, bonds slide as Treasury buyback disappoints, oil tops $100
By David Shepardson and Dan Catchpole
WASHINGTON, Sept 9 (Reuters) - One pilot of the Amazon Prime Air cargo plane that crashed in Miami on Sunday cautioned they were flying "too fast" just over a minute before touching down on the runway they overran, the National Transportation Safety Board said.
The pilot continued to comment on the plane’s speed while automated warnings sounded in the cockpit.
However, the other pilot did not give a clear verbal response, according to the cockpit voice recording detailed in an investigative update on Wednesday that did not identify the speakers as the captain or first officer.
The 32-year-old Boeing 767 operated by Miami-based 21 Air overran the runway by some 1,300 feet (396 m) and crashed into two vehicles on the ground, killing five people and injuring another five.
Before the plane touched down, "sink rate sink rate" rang out twice in the cockpit as the aircraft at one point descended 400 feet in just four seconds, based on the information released by the NTSB. That was followed by five warnings of "too low terrain."
"The big question is, why did they continue their approach?" said Anthony Brickhouse, an aerospace safety consultant. "They had several cues that their approach was not stable, but they continued instead of going around."
Fifteen seconds after touching down, one of the pilots called for aborting the landing and the engine throttles were increased to a value consistent with go-around thrust, the NTSB said.
At this point the plane was nearing the end of the runway but still travelling at 120 knots (138 mph), according to data from Flightradar24 based on initial NTSB disclosures.
But four seconds later, the throttles were reduced to idle power and there were then sounds similar to the plane departing the runway’s paved surface, the NTSB said.
The board said on Tuesday there was no indication in the recorded data that speed brakes or thrust reversers were deployed to help slow the plane.
21 Air did not respond immediately to a request for comment on the information released by the NTSB.
Safety experts say most airplane accidents are caused by multiple factors that need to be thoroughly investigated.
"From what I’ve seen so far, there was definitely a breakdown in crew resource management," Brickhouse said, referring to training pilots receive to communicate clearly and coordinate decisions in the cockpit.
When a pilot ignores cues that something is wrong, "unfortunately, bad things happen," he added. "So as an investigator, I want to know with that many cues available, what was their motivation? What was their thought process? Why did they continue that approach instead of going around?"
NTSB investigators spent much of Wednesday interviewing the captain and first officer before releasing details from the cockpit voice recorder.
The Amazon cargo plane was on its third flight of the day, coming from San Juan, Puerto Rico. It had flown from Cincinnati to Miami and from Miami to San Juan earlier on Sunday before the crash at 1:53 p.m. EDT (1753 GMT).
The captain, 55, received his type rating for the 767 in May and has 7,145 hours of flight time, while the first officer, 37, received his type rating on the 767 in April 2025 and has 2,655 flight hours, the NTSB said on Tuesday.

title: Asian currencies steady as risk-off tone weighs, yen holds near highs
full_text:
U.S. stocks end lower, bonds slide as Treasury buyback disappoints, oil tops $100
Asian currencies were largely steady on Thursday as a risk-off tone dominated markets, with the Japanese yen holding near recent highs while the U.S. dollar steadied. Rising oil prices and renewed Middle East tensions kept investors cautious ahead of Friday’s U.S. inflation report.
The USD/JPY pair was around 153.47, after the yen strengthened to 152.89 on Tuesday, its strongest level since February, before easing.
The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics will publish August producer prices later on Thursday, followed by consumer-price data on Friday. The U.S. dollar index fell marginally to 98.76.
Dollar steadies as oil tops $100, Fed hike bets hold
Brent crude climbed as high as $101.94 a barrel before paring gains and remained above $100, as Iran said it was prepared for a more intense war with the United States.
The latest escalation followed the biggest wave of attacks on shipping by both sides since the start of the conflict, raising the risk of further disruption to Middle East energy supplies.
Iran has no intention of backing down despite a U.S. naval blockade and attacks on its oil tankers, according to a senior Iranian official. The official said economic pain may be increasing, but Tehran sees the conflict as an existential threat and has little choice but to continue fighting.
Higher oil prices are adding to inflation pressure already reflected in higher bond yields. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield held near 4.85%, its highest level since late 2023, after the Treasury said it would buy up to $6 billion of longer-dated debt, a move that disappointed investors who had expected a larger increase.
Swaps now imply about a 62% chance of a Fed quarter-point hike at the September 15-16 meeting, up from 60% on Tuesday.
Yen rally pauses as BOJ tightening bets remain firm
The yen edged higher to around 153.50 per dollar after rising 0.3% Wednesday following pressure from U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
The rally has now paused after the currency’s powerful gains pushed it to a seven-month high earlier this week.
Markets broadly expect the BOJ to raise rates by 25 basis points on September 18, with the outcome of Friday’s U.S. inflation report likely to influence the yen through the dollar and interest-rate gap.
The yen’s gains have been driven by several factors, including expectations for faster BOJ tightening, possible repatriation of Japanese funds and the unwinding of carry trades.
The latest move has also kept intervention risks in focus after Japan’s record currency support last month.
Yuan firm as China inflation rebounds, rupee faces oil pressure
The USD/CNH pair and the USD/CNY pair was little changed. The offshore yuan remained near its strongest level in nearly four years after Chinese consumer and producer prices rose in August, driven in part by higher energy costs.
The Indian rupee faced renewed pressure from higher oil prices. The USD/INR pair was around 95.16, with traders expecting the Reserve Bank of India’s support to temper rather than reverse the currency’s decline.
Elsewhere, the USD/KRW pair fell marginally to 1,339.35, while the USD/SGD pair rose 0.02% to 1.26.
The USD/AUD pair was around 1.39, implying an Australian dollar near $0.72. The USD/NZD pair was around 1.71, implying a kiwi near $0.58.

title: Trump on Iran war; Oracle, Adobe to report - what’s moving markets
full_text:
U.S. stocks end lower, bonds slide as Treasury buyback disappoints, oil tops $100
Investing.com - Futures linked to the main U.S. stock indices point up with elevated oil prices and a raft of crucial economic data in focus. U.S. President Donald Trump says the Iran war will end after the U.S. midterm elections in November, even as his top advisers reportedly tell him the conflict could stretch until his term in the White House concludes in early 2029. Earnings from Oracle and Adobe could offer new insight into the impact of the artificial intelligence boom, while the European Central Bank is expected to lift interest rates after its latest policy gathering.
1. Futures rise
U.S. stock futures edged higher on Thursday, as investors assessed ongoing tensions in the Middle East and geared up for key economic data later in the week.
By 03:02 ET (07:02 GMT), the Dow futures contract had gained 213 points, or 0.4%, S&P 500 futures had risen by 18 points, or 0.2%, and Nasdaq 100 futures had ticked up by 15 points, or 0.1%.
The main averages on Wall Street retreated in the prior session, weighed down by further violence between the U.S. and Iran, which exacerbated concerns over a prolonged closure of the critical Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude prices, the global benchmark, surpassed $100 a barrel for the first time since July, fueling worries over an energy-driven inflation wave and central bank policy tightening. Fresh readings of producer and consumer price growth are set to released this week.
Sparked by the oil price jump, as well as news that the Treasury Department will repurchase less in government bonds in its latest operation than some analysts had hoped, U.S. Treasury yields climbed. The benchmark 10-year yield, in particular, hit a post-2023 high of 4.84%. Yields tend to move inversely to prices.
Risk assets, in turn, were came under pressure, with the S&P 500 dropping to for a third straight session.
“So even though we’re just over a week into September, it’s already living up to its reputation as one of the toughest months of the year for markets,” analysts at Deutsche Banks said in a note.
In individual stocks, shares of Apple ended lower after the tech giant unveiled a $1,999 passport-shaped foldable version of its flagship iPhone device.
2. Iran war to end after midterms, Trump says
Despite the U.S. and Iran exchanging retaliatory air strikes in recent days, President Donald Trump told supporters at a rally on Wednesday that the conflict would end after the U.S. midterm elections in November.
Although the president himself is not on the ballot, polls have suggested that the Iran war has dented Trump’s popularity and threatened to impact the midterm results of his Republican Party. Voters have been especially frustrated with a spike in gasoline pump prices following the outbreak of the fighting in late February.
Trump accused Tehran of attempting to influence the vote, which could see the Republican lose control over Congress -- an outcome which could have implications for the White House’s policy objectives both at home and abroad.
Previously, Trump has set deadlines to end the war, while an interim ceasefire deal signed in June proved to be short-lived. According to the Wall Street Journal, Trump’s top advisers have warned him that the conflict could extend until through the rest of his presidency, which is due to conclude in January 2029.
3. Oracle to report
On the earnings calendar, markets will turn their attention to returns from Oracle after the closing bell on Thursday.
Earlier this year, the cloud computing giant has outlined plans to spend heavily and raise more debt, as it races to build out its artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Oracle has secured major deals, including with megacap technology player Meta Platforms and ChatGPT-maker OpenAI, all with the hope of challenging cloud peers like Microsoft and Amazon in harnessing AI.
In June, Oracle said it expects to cobble together around $40 billion from a combination of debt and equity financing next year, up from a prior at-the-market equity issuance of $20 billion. Capital expenditures, meanwhile, were forecast at $95 billion in fiscal 2027, compared to analysts' expectations of $67.66 billion, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters.
4. Adobe earnings ahead
Elsewhere, Adobe is also due to unveil results after U.S. markets close on Thursday.
The earnings will be the first since the Photoshop-maker announced the exit of CFO Dan Durn in June, which further fanned worries around the company's strategy to both fend off design rivals and fold AI into its offerings.
Earlier this year, CEO Shantanu Narayen stepped down as well, leaving Adobe's leadership mired in uncertainty.
Still, Adobe raised its annual revenue and profit outlook, possibly underlining solid demand for Adobe's AI products and tools despite threats to market share posed by design upstarts like Figma and Canva. AI-first annual recurring revenue topped $500 million at the end of the second quarter.

From summer pause to fully baked 25 bps hike

ECB guidance & upcoming U.S. inflation test

title: Trump offers $5,000 to every American if Republicans win midterm elections
full_text:
U.S. stocks end lower, bonds slide as Treasury buyback disappoints, oil tops $100
By Nandita Bose, Steve Holland and Nathan Layne
DALLAS, Sept 9 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Wednesday he would pay every American adult a $5,000 "Trump dividend" if Republicans retain control of Congress in November’s midterm election, an extraordinary attempt to persuade voters to back his party.
Trump made the proposal at his Republican Party’s first-ever midterm convention, but it was not immediately clear how the payments would work or whether they would be legal. With approximately 270 million U.S. adults, the idea would cost around $1.35 trillion.
During a primetime address that lasted an hour and 45 minutes, Trump boasted of completing "the greatest two years in the history of the presidency," putting himself squarely at the center of the election despite his deepening unpopularity.
But it was not clear whether his campaign-style speech would appeal to the critical swing voters who opinion polls show have drifted away from Trump’s party, amid growing dissatisfaction with the cost of living and the war on Iran.
"We hand America’s future to the radical left Democrats, and our nation will spend the next decade just getting back on its feet," he said. "Vote Republicans and we will leave the world in our dust for generations to come."
The two-day Dallas gathering, where Trump will also deliver the closing remarks on Thursday after Vice President JD Vance’s keynote address, underscores the extent to which Republicans’ fortunes are tethered to Trump and serves as a showcase for their strategy ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
The event was so centered on the president that Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters informally dubbed it "Trumpapalooza," a nod to the popular Lollapalooza music festival.
The focus on Trump amounts to a risky bet that he can mobilize the voters who carried him to the presidency two years ago, despite public polls showing his approval ratings have hit an all-time low. The president vowed to pay multiple visits to battleground states and districts in the eight weeks until Election Day.
"I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot," Trump said, a line that may have pleased Democratic campaign strategists just as much as MAGA voters.
The convention presented a tough choice in particular for Republicans facing difficult elections who may need to distance themselves from the president to broaden their appeal but cannot afford to alienate Trump’s most committed supporters.
Many such Republicans skipped the convention, including Representative Tom Barrett of Michigan, Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska and Senator Susan Collins of Maine, all facing strong Democratic challengers this fall.
Some, however, elected to travel to Dallas. At least 16 candidates in competitive House and Senate races were scheduled to speak, according to the RNC schedule. Among those who spoke on Wednesday were Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a close Trump ally who is locked in a tough Senate race with Democratic lawmaker James Talarico, and Ohio Senator Jon Husted, who faces former Senator Sherrod Brown.
Though Trump insisted the 21,000-seat arena was "packed," the upper sections remained largely empty during his speech capping Wednesday’s program.
DEMOCRATS PORTRAYED AS ’SOCIALISTS’ AND ’COMMUNISTS’
While Republican officials had described the convention as an opportunity to tout Trump’s policies, most of the early speakers focused largely on attacking Democrats as extreme on topics such as transgender women in sports and border security – political red meat for the base.
Issues that voters have consistently cited as top concerns, the Iran war and the cost of living, received comparatively less attention.
Alabama state Representative Ernie Yarbrough, a convention attendee, said Trump needs to give voters a clearer sense of how long the war in Iran could last and what the administration’s aims are.
"People want to feel like we’re not getting stuck in an endless cycle," he said.
Trump defended his decision to attack Tehran, saying he acted to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. He also promised that oil prices would drop "as soon as we win the war with Iran," which he vowed would happen soon.
But the conflict shows little sign of ending more than six months after the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran, and analysts have said Iran’s nuclear program has not been eliminated. Iran denies seeking a nuclear weapon.
Before Trump took the stage, a parade of speakers called Democrats "socialists" and "communists," echoing one of Trump’s favorite attack lines following a handful of victories by democratic socialists in Democratic primary elections.
Democrats are "dangerous, radical and weird," said Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina, the chairman of the party’s Senate campaign arm.
Wednesday’s program also featured a surprise pretaped video from Democratic U.S. Senator John Fetterman, who introduced his fellow senator from Pennsylvania, Republican Dave McCormick, as his "great friend" while declaring he would work with Trump to protect the state’s steel industry.
Fetterman’s extraordinary participation appeared likely to emphasize the ideological divides plaguing the Democratic Party ahead of the midterms. Fetterman, who has increasingly clashed with left-wing Democrats, has denied speculation that he may leave the party.
The convention’s stakes are high for both parties. With the elections less than two months away, Republicans face the prospect of losing control of at least one chamber of Congress, with public polling showing Democrats more motivated to vote and Trump’s approval ratings deeply underwater.
The event faced stiff competition for viewers with the start of the NFL season, with opening night coinciding with a Super Bowl rematch between the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks.
Still, after months of negative headlines over the Iran war and inflation, many Republicans see the gathering as their best chance to promote candidates, draw contrasts with Democrats and energize a Republican electorate expressing less enthusiasm about voting than Democrats, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll.

title: U.S. consumer price growth seen rising 0.3% month-on-month in August - Truflation
full_text:
U.S. stocks end lower, bonds slide as Treasury buyback disappoints, oil tops $100
Investing.com - U.S. consumer price growth is expected to have accelerated in August, indicating that the inflation picture is becoming “more complex” ahead of the Federal Reserve’s upcoming interest rate decision, according to estimates from Truflation.
In a report seen by Investing.com, the independent inflation index expects Friday’s headline official consumer price index from the Labor Department to come in at 0.3% month-on-month. In July, the figure rose by just 0.1%.
Stripping out volatile items like food and fuel, so-called “core” CPI is anticipated to increase by 0.2%, in line with July.
If realized, this would see headline inflation holding steady at 3.4% in the 12 months to August, while core CPI would slow slightly to 2.4% year-on-year, Truflation projected.
“The main upside driver” for headline inflation is likely to stem from higher gasoline prices, Truflation said. Escalating tensions in the Iran war and the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz have caused energy prices to once again surge, pushing up gas prices for American consumers by 3.4% in August -- a key month in the typically busy summer travel period.
Retail fuel prices floated above $4 per gallon last month and topped $4.10 in early September, up nearly a dollar from a year earlier, according to data from price-tracking service GasBuddy cited by Reuters.
“Combined with tight gasoline inventories, this leaves little buffer against further disruptions, meaning pump prices are unlikely to deliver meaningful relief unless crude prices ease or domestic inventories rebuild,” Truflation said.
U.S. President Donald Trump has promised to slash expenses at the pump, although he flagged in August that Americans should be willing to pay a “tiny little bit more” for gasoline to support his effort to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Brent crude futures surpassed $100 a barrel for the first time since July on Wednesday.
Truflation suggested that downward momentum in apparel prices helped to mitigate price growth in August, as retailers leaned into back-to-school sales and end-of-summer promotions to entice increasingly cost-sensitive shoppers. But the discounting may have only pulled down prices in the short term, especially in the wake of recent tariff and import cost pressures, Truflation said.
The group also predicted that the next phase of inflation is likely to be shaped by an “increasingly divergent outlook for goods and services.”
“Looking ahead, the key question is whether rising tariffs, import and producer costs push goods inflation higher, while wage growth, productivity and labor market conditions determine the persistence of services inflation,” Truflation wrote.
The trajectory of inflation has been front of mind for markets, especially as many Fed policymakers have indicated that they will prioritize corralling prices ahead of the central bank’s two-day meeting next week. In a speech at the Fed’s Jackson Hole symposium late last month, Chair Kevin Warsh also suggested that, despite better inflation readings this summer, the underlying trend has not improved.
Meanwhile, blockbuster August jobs data appeared to reinforce the view among some investors that the labor market was robust enough to withstand a rate increase. In theory, raising interest rates can help quell inflation, albeit at the risk of weighing on broader economic growth.
Traders are now wagering a roughly 60% chance that the Fed will lift borrowing costs by a quarter of a percentage point this month, up from 40% a week ago, according to CME’s FedWatch Tool.
“[T]he markets are pricing in a rate hike, but much of the current rise in inflation is driven by oil prices, so it may be seen as temporary and, as a result,” the Fed could opt to leave rates unchanged, said Oliver Rust, Head of Data at Truflation.

title: China AI chipmakers hike prices as HBM shortage hits domestic push - Reuters
full_text:
U.S. stocks end lower, bonds slide as Treasury buyback disappoints, oil tops $100
Investing.com -- Chinese AI chipmakers including Huawei Technologies and Cambricon Technologies have raised prices for current and next-generation processors as a global shortage of high-bandwidth memory squeezes the cost of building domestic alternatives to Nvidia, Reuters reported on Thursday.
Huawei has raised the indicated price of its Ascend 950DT accelerator card to more than 250,000 yuan ($37,255), up 20% to 50% from quotes given customers about two months ago, depending on contract terms, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Cambricon has also lifted the indicated price of its planned 690 chip by 20% to 30%, while smaller rivals MetaX and Iluvatar CoreX have made similar increases, the sources said.
Cambricon shares were last down about 0.6% at 1,049 yuan on Thursday, while Iluvatar CoreX fell about 2% to HK$325.40. Cambricon's stock had already dropped 3.1% on Tuesday and 0.4% on Wednesday, while Iluvatar CoreX has fallen sharply in recent sessions.
The price increases highlight a growing constraint for China's effort to build a self-sufficient AI-computing ecosystem. HBM is a critical component in AI accelerators because its vertically stacked memory allows processors to access large amounts of data at very high speeds.
The advanced HBM market is dominated by South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics and U.S.-based Micron Technology.
Beijing wants Chinese companies to replace Nvidia processors, but more expensive HBM raises the price of the very domestic accelerators intended to fill that gap. Huawei's Ascend 950 series is due to become available in the fourth quarter, while Cambricon's 690 has not yet formally launched.
The pricing pressure is not confined to new products. Huawei's Ascend 950PR, which sold for about 60,000 yuan per card at the start of 2026, now fetches more than 80,000 yuan, while its older Ascend 910C board has risen to more than 110,000 yuan from roughly 90,000 yuan, according to the sources cited by Reuters.
The shortage is also forcing Chinese suppliers to prioritize customers. Iluvatar CoreX has doubled its planned GPU shipments to ByteDance to 100,000 units this year, according to Reuters, while also diverting GPUs that had been intended for its own use.
Huawei remains ByteDance's largest domestic supplier, followed by Cambricon and Iluvatar CoreX, the sources told Reuters.

Belron, the windscreen repair and replacement unit in which D’Ieteren holds a 50.3% fully diluted stake, drove most of the group’s first-half gain.
Its adjusted profit before tax, group share, rose 28.6% to €308.2 million, with an adjusted operating margin of 23%, up 160 basis points year on year. Free cash flow surged 89% to €485.1 million, supported by strong operating performance and lower financial charges.
D’Ieteren Automotive, the fully owned Belgian vehicle distributor, weighed on results. Its adjusted profit before tax, group share, fell 66.6% to €36.4 million as sales dropped 10.8% to €2.27 billion, hit by lower volumes and a negative price-mix effect that compressed the adjusted operating margin to 2.1% from 4.5% a year earlier. Management said automotive trends are not expected to improve in the second half.
The unit announced a transformation plan that could result in the loss of 344 jobs and recognized a €47.2 million goodwill impairment charge on its retail operations.
Parts distribution unit PHE posted an 18.4% rise in adjusted profit before tax, group share, to €106.8 million on sales up 10.4% to €1.61 billion, including one month of contribution from two recently acquired Spanish distributors.
TVH, the agricultural and industrial equipment parts distributor, reported adjusted profit before tax, group share, up 16.9% to €44.2 million on sales up 5.3% to €894.8 million.
Moleskine, the notebook brand, improved its adjusted profit before tax, group share, to negative €4.7 million from negative €7.6 million a year earlier on sales up 2.2% to €52.2 million, aided by lower financial charges following a €76.4 million shareholder loan waiver.
The corporate and unallocated segment held net financial debt of €299.8 million at end-June, or €486.6 million excluding inter-segment loans.

title: US trial against China’s Huawei opens with prosecutor calling the company a criminal enterprise
full_text:
U.S. stocks end lower, bonds slide as Treasury buyback disappoints, oil tops $100
By Karen Freifeld
NEW YORK, Sept 9 (Reuters) - A U.S. prosecutor described China’s Huawei as a criminal enterprise that stole from American companies to build its telecommunications empire, as the trial against the tech giant kicked off in Brooklyn federal court on Wednesday.
"Theft, lies, cover-up," Taylor Stout, a trial attorney from the U.S. Department of Justice, said in the government’s opening statement. "For 20 years, that’s how Huawei, a massive Chinese telecommunications company, victimized American companies and abused the American financial system, all in an effort to dominate the telecommunications industry around the world."
Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from five U.S. companies, including operating system source code for internet routers from Cisco Systems and a robotic arm to test phones from T-Mobile, to gain an unfair competitive advantage and grow its business, the prosecutor told jurors.
"We’ll hear from people who caught Huawei red-handed trying to steal American tech," Stout said, adding there was video of an employee stealing the robotic arm.
The defense painted a very different picture of the company and its success in court.
"It’s about competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct," Brian Heberlig, one of a team of lawyers representing Huawei, said in his opening. "Huawei earned its success ... There was no blueprint for crime."
Huawei is known for its telecommunications equipment, mobile phones and, in recent years, AI chips. It does business globally but its networking gear is restricted in the U.S. and suppliers are banned from exporting U.S. goods and technology to the company without approval from the Department of Commerce.
On Thursday, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said "the Chinese government firmly opposes the U.S. side’s suppression and containment of Chinese enterprises," when asked about the case and the American prosecutor’s "criminal enterprise" description.
China "firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests," the spokesperson said at a regular press conference.
DEFENSE SAYS GOVERNMENT ’CHERRY-PICKING’
The case against Huawei began in 2018 with an indictment charging the company and its chief financial officer with bank fraud and sanctions violations for allegedly misrepresenting its business in Iran to get around U.S. sanctions and move millions of dollars through the U.S. financial system.
In the ensuing years, it grew into a sprawling indictment that includes racketeering, a pattern of illegal activity conducted by an enterprise to generate profit.
Heberlig, defending Huawei, told jurors that prosecutors will describe routine activities by global tech companies "but will twist those ordinary activities to try to make them look criminal."
The government was "cherry-picking isolated events that should not be viewed as evidence of an overarching conspiracy that never existed," he said.
He said the incidents involving Cisco and T-mobile were "actions by individual employees" and that management worked to make things right after learning of them. Another incident in which an employee took unauthorized photos of a Fujitsu networking device at a trade show was a "foolish act" by one employee who was "promptly fired," the defense attorney said.
The prosecutor also accused the company of keeping the nature of its work in Iran secret, so it could launder U.S. dollars through the financial system and could help the Iranian government spy on its own citizens.
The defense said there was no evidence Huawei knew the dollar-clearing would violate U.S. sanctions law and that the company could have kept it outside the U.S. or in another currency. He also said the banks allegedly misled by Huawei knew about its business in Iran and still competed for its business.
In 2018, Huawei’s chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou, was detained in Vancouver after being picked up on a U.S. warrant as a part of the original indictment. She fought extradition for nearly three years before being freed to return to China in a diplomatic agreement between the U.S., China and Canada.
The charges against her were dismissed in 2022 as part of a deferred prosecution agreement but admissions she made are set to be introduced as evidence at the trial, which is expected to last three months.
The criminal case is based in part on reporting by Reuters in 2012 and 2013 about close ties between Huawei and Skycom, a firm that operated in Iran.
Reuters reported that Skycom had offered to sell at least €1.3 million ($1.5 million) worth of embargoed Hewlett-Packard computer equipment to Iran’s largest mobile-phone operator in 2010. Reuters also reported that Meng had served on Skycom’s board of directors between February 2008 and April 2009.
